🔢 Solving Rav Mattana's Count — why the mishna only tallies cases that could lead toward sin-offering liability
📜 'When He Does It' — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's proof that two people acting together are exempt
🎒 A Body Laden With Food — is carrying it out like lifting an object with one's hand?
✋ Whose Domain Is a Hand? — Abaye proves it is neither public nor private
🍎 The Hand Full of Fruit — five ways the Gemara reconciles two contradictory baraitot

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Exemptions, a Laden Body, and a Wandering Hand
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 3a–3b
overview.hebrewSource: כֹּל פְּטוּרֵי דְשַׁבָּת פָּטוּר אֲבָל אָסוּר, בַּר מֵהָנֵי תְּלָת דְּפָטוּר וּמוּתָּר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Daf 3 opens by using Shmuel's rule — that nearly every exempt ruling on Shabbat is nonetheless rabbinically prohibited — to sharpen the previous daf's open question about counting the mishna's cases. The Gemara then defends the mishna's ruling that two people who together complete one prohibited labor are both exempt, rooting it in the verse's word 'בַּעֲשֹׂתָהּ.' From there it moves to Rav's dilemma about a person laden with food across his body rather than in his hand, and Abaye's proof that an outstretched hand belongs to no fixed domain. The daf closes with an extended, multi-layered attempt to reconcile two baraitot that disagree about whether one may bring a fruit-filled hand back after extending it into the public domain.

slides.title: 🦌 Exempt But Prohibited — Except for Three
slides.subtitle: Shmuel's rule, and the narrow exceptions to it

boxes.title: The General Rule (Shmuel)
items: Almost every exempt ruling in the halakhot of Shabbat is 'exempt but prohibited'
Torah law imposes no liability, but the Sages forbade the act anyway
This applies whenever a defined action was actually performed

boxes.title: Three True Exceptions
items: 🦌 Trapping a deer — sitting at the entrance of a house it already entered on its own
🐍 Trapping a poisonous snake — permitted because of the danger it poses
🩹 Draining an abscess — lancing a boil to relieve the pus

callout.label: Why these three:
callout.text: Even Shmuel's cases are 'exempt but prohibited' when a defined action was performed; these three were singled out precisely because they ARE defined actions that the Sages nonetheless permitted outright.

slides.title: 🔢 Solving Rav Mattana's Count
slides.subtitle: Why the mishna's total stays at eight, not twelve

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav Mattana's challenge stands: the mishna's second half has four 'both exempt' cases, each really performed by two separate people
2️⃣ The Gemara answers: only cases where the person performed an act of lifting (עֲקִירָה) are counted, because lifting can lead toward sin-offering liability if the act continues
3️⃣ Under no circumstances can one who merely places an object come to violate a more serious prohibition — placing alone is a dead end, halakhically
4️⃣ So the mishna's tally counts liftings, not participants — which is why the total remains eight cases, not twelve

callout.label: Principle:
callout.text: The mishna's bookkeeping tracks potential paths to greater liability, not the raw number of people whose hands were involved.

slides.title: 📜 'When He Does It' — And a Body Laden With Food
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi grounds the mishna's exemption, then Rav tests its limits

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: The mishna's second half rules 'both exempt' — but a severe Torah prohibition WAS carried out between the two of them! How can both go free?

lines.speaker:
Rabbi Yehuda
HaNasi
lines.text: Leviticus 4:27 says one who sins is liable בַּעֲשֹׂתָהּ — 'when he does it.' One who performs the whole transgression is liable; one who performs only part of it is not.

lines.speaker: Rav
lines.text: If another person loaded me with food and drink across my back, and I walked out with it — is moving my whole body like lifting the object with my hand? Am I liable?

lines.speaker:
Rabbi Yehuda
HaNasi
lines.text: Liable — and it is not comparable to the case of a hand merely holding an object. A body comes to rest in a fixed place; a hand does not.

callout.label: The distinction:
callout.text: גּוּפוֹ נָיַיח, יָדוֹ לָא נָיַיח — 'his body is at rest, his hand is not.' A laden body counts as an act of lifting in a way a mere hand does not.

slides.title: ✋ Whose Domain Is a Hand?
slides.subtitle: Abaye proves an outstretched hand belongs to neither domain

nodes.content: ❓ Abaye: is a person's hand, once extended into a different domain, considered part of that domain — or of the one he stands in?

columns.label: Not like the public domain
columns.content: The poor person's hand carrying an object INTO the private domain: if the homeowner takes it, the homeowner is not liable. Were the hand 'public domain,' this would be a full transfer.

columns.label: Not like the private domain
columns.content: The homeowner's hand carrying an object OUT to the public domain: if the poor person takes it, the poor person is not liable, for the identical reason.

nodes.content: ✅ Conclusion: an outstretched hand is legally neither the public domain nor the private domain — it belongs to neither

callout.label: What's next:
callout.text: This sets up Abaye's own dilemma — while hanging between domains, does the hand instead take on the status of a karmelit?

slides.title: 🍎 A Hand Full of Fruit — Five Attempted Resolutions
slides.subtitle: Two baraitot disagree: may one bring a fruit-filled hand back after extending it outside?
rows: Hand extended above ten handbreadths (outside the public domain's airspace)
Hand extended below ten handbreadths (within the public domain)
Hand extended while it was still day, before Shabbat began
Hand extended after dark, once Shabbat had already begun
Sages did not penalize an unwitting act on account of intentional ones
Sages DID penalize it, lest people come to act intentionally
Returning it to the SAME courtyard he stood in
Returning it to a DIFFERENT courtyard

callout.label: Rava's version:
callout.text: Same courtyard — since his goal of moving the fruit elsewhere was never achieved, forcing him to bring it back is itself a kind of penalty. Different courtyard — his goal WAS achieved, so the Sages prohibit completing the transfer.

summary.principle: Liability for carrying requires a defined act of lifting by one person acting alone; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives the exemption for joint action from 'בַּעֲשֹׂתָהּ,' and the Gemara works through several ways to explain when the Sages did or did not penalize a hand extended, fruit-filled, into another domain.

flowSteps.content: 🦌 Shmuel: nearly all exempt Shabbat rulings are still rabbinically prohibited, except three defined cases
🔢 Rav Mattana's count is resolved: the mishna tallies only acts of LIFTING, since only lifting can lead toward greater liability
📜 Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: 'בַּעֲשֹׂתָהּ' — one who does the WHOLE act is liable; two who split it are exempt

columns.content: 🎒 A laden body IS liable, unlike a mere hand, since the body comes to rest and the hand does not
✋ Abaye: an outstretched hand belongs to neither the public nor the private domain

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: a Torah violation of carrying requires ONE person's complete act of lifting and placing — everything else is measured against that standard

quiz.q: According to Shmuel, what is the general rule for rulings of 'exempt' in the halakhot of Shabbat?
o: They are always fully permitted
They are exempt from a sin-offering but still rabbinically prohibited
They only apply to priests
They apply only on Yom Kippur
quiz.e: Shmuel taught that nearly every exempt ruling on Shabbat carries no Torah liability but is nonetheless prohibited by the Sages, with three narrow exceptions.

quiz.q: Which of the following is one of Shmuel's three exceptions that are 'exempt and permitted'?
o: Carrying a house key
Trapping a poisonous snake, because of the danger it poses
Reciting the evening Shema late
Baking bread before Shabbat
quiz.e: The three exceptions are trapping a deer that already entered a house, trapping a poisonous snake due to the danger, and draining an abscess.

quiz.q: What verse does Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi cite to explain why two people who together perform one prohibited labor are both exempt?
o: "When you lie down and when you arise" (Deut. 6:7)
"There was evening and there was morning" (Genesis 1)
"...when he does it" (בַּעֲשֹׂתָהּ, Leviticus 4:27), read to require doing the entire act alone
"You shall not kindle a fire" (Exodus 35:3)
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives from the word בַּעֲשֹׂתָהּ that only one who performs the complete transgression alone is liable; a joint act by two people exempts both.

quiz.q: Why does Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rule that a person laden with food and drink across his body, who then walks out, IS liable — unlike a person who merely carried an object in his hand?
o: Because carrying on one's back is a greater sin
Because the body comes to rest in a defined place, while a hand does not
Because only priests may carry with their hands
Because his friend was also involved
quiz.e: The distinguishing principle is גּוּפוֹ נָיַיח, יָדוֹ לָא נָיַיח — the body settles into a fixed place, so moving it counts as lifting, while a hand does not.

quiz.q: What did Abaye prove about a person's hand once it is extended into a different domain holding an object?
o: That it always takes on the status of the domain it entered
That it is legally neither the public domain nor the private domain
That it becomes ownerless property
That it is always considered a karmelit
quiz.e: Abaye proved from the mishna's own rulings — that neither the homeowner nor the poor person becomes liable when merely receiving from an extended hand — that the hand itself belongs to neither domain.
